Bresnahan, MD Anderson Cancer Center (Bhattacharya Lab) 2026-11-11 Home placenta-xqtl-federated lets cohorts with placental RNA-seq and genotype data take part in a multi-ancestry placental xQTL study without sharing individual-level data. Each cohort runs the pipeline on its own computers and sends only summary-level files (A–J) to MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC), which combines them across cohorts and ancestry groups. Pipeline version: 1.0.0-dev. These pages are built from the docs/ folder of the repository; the same pages are included inside the pipeline image for offline reading. Where to start Cohort investigators: read the Collaboration brief for the aims, the analyses each site runs and the files requested. Analysts running the pipeline: start with the quick start below, then the HPC configuration guide. Maintainers: the appendix Testing and validation describes the automated tests, the cluster checks on seadragon and the release checks. Quick start The pipeline is distributed as one self-contained image (software, public reference data, Java and Nextflow). It needs no internet access at the site. apptainer pull xqtl-federated_<version>.sif oras://ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:<version> sha256sum -c xqtl-federated_<version>.sif.sha256 apptainer run xqtl-federated_<version>.sif bootstrap ./xqtl ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon,smoke ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon -params-file cohort.yml --mode prepare_references ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon -params-file cohort.yml --mode site Replace seadragon with your scheduler and engine, for example -profile slurm,apptainer -c mysite.config (see Executors). The restricted file Site runs need xqtl-restricted-<version>.tar.gz, a small file that holds the shared splicing clusters and the MDACC signal list. MDACC sends it by email after the data-sharing agreement is approved. If your site has not received it, request it from the scientific contact, Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org), stating your cohort, the pipeline version and the approved agreement. Do not redistribute it. Licence The pipeline is GPL-3.0. Collaboration brief Collaboration brief: proposed analyses and summary files requested from participating cohorts Project: Multi-ancestry placental xQTL meta-analysis Prepared for: Participating placental cohort investigators, including PACEplacenta collaborators Coordinating institution: MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC), Bhattacharya Lab Scientific contact: Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org) Analysis software: MDACC-provided self-contained pipeline (first release in preparation) 1. Purpose of the collaboration We are studying how fetal genetic differences affect RNA produced by the placenta and whether conditions during pregnancy, such as maternal glucose levels or BMI, change those effects. We will combine results from cohorts with different genetic ancestries to identify placental genes and RNA forms that may be relevant to birth outcomes and childhood metabolic health. \[1, 2\] For cohorts that cannot transfer participant-level data to MDACC, each cohort runs the analyses on its own computing system. It reviews the summary files and sends MDACC only those approved under its data-sharing rules. No participant-level genotypes, RNA-seq files, molecular measurements, or clinical records are sent to MDACC. Separately, each site must upload quality-controlled genotype files to the external TOPMed Imputation Server, as described in Section 5. Cohorts able to share de-identified individual-level data may discuss a separate arrangement with MDACC under an appropriate agreement. This document describes the planned analyses, what each cohort would run locally, what MDACC would do with the shared results, and which files sites would send. The final section lists possible later analyses that would require discussion with collaborators before any additional work or data sharing. 2. Research questions and planned analyses 2.1 Identify genetic effects on different RNA measurements We aim to identify genetic variants that affect placental RNA measurements, including changes that gene-level expression alone may miss. Using a placenta-specific reference built from long-read RNA sequencing (HPLRv2), participating sites will measure nine types of RNA features: gene expression, isoform expression, isoform usage, splicing, intron retention, alternative transcription start sites, alternative polyadenylation, RNA editing, and RNA stability. For each RNA feature, sites will test which nearby fetal genetic variants are associated with its measurement (cis-xQTL analysis), separately for each eligible ancestry group. The analyses will also identify independent genetic signals within each region. \[3, 4\] Sites will estimate the proportions of major placental cell types using a public single-cell RNA reference. These estimates will be included in the statistical models to account for differences among samples. At significant xQTL signals from the site’s own analysis, and at a list of xQTL signals supplied by MDACC, sites will also test whether the genetic association changes with the proportion of a cell type, such as trophoblast, endothelial, or stromal cells. \[5\] MDACC will combine association results across cohorts and ancestry groups to identify consistent and varying genetic effects. We will also use each cohort’s linkage disequilibrium (LD) results, which describe correlations among nearby genetic variants, to narrow the list of candidate causal variants across ancestries. \[6\] 2.2 Compare placental findings with birth and childhood health studies We will integrate placental xQTL results with publicly available genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for birth weight, gestational duration, childhood BMI and anthropometric traits, glycemic phenotypes, and youth-onset type 2 diabetes. Planned analyses include statistical fine-mapping, colocalization to assess whether placental xQTL and GWAS signals may share causal variants, and transcriptome-wide association analyses (TWAS), which use genetic evidence to prioritize genes and RNA isoforms. Functional annotation will further characterize credible variants and candidate regulatory mechanisms. \[7–12\] These analyses use association summaries and LD matrices shared by sites, together with published GWAS results. They do not require sites to release participant-level childhood outcomes or other participant-level clinical data to MDACC. More advanced methods, including multivariate isoform-level TWAS, will be added after we confirm that they work with summary statistics from separate cohorts. 2.3 Test whether pregnancy conditions modify genetic effects Genotype-by-exposure (GxE) analysis will test whether the association between fetal genotype and placental RNA phenotypes changes with gestational exposures. The initial local workflow includes genotype-by-gestational-age interaction scans and, where sufficiently measured and permitted, interactions with pre-pregnancy BMI, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) glucose. Exposure variables remain at the cohort site; only interaction statistics and aggregate exposure descriptors are requested. \[13\] In the first release, sites will run interaction tests separately for each eligible ancestry group. MDACC will combine results from cohorts with comparable exposures and models. Planned extensions will examine more extensive interaction statistics, colocalization of exposure-modified signals with GWAS loci, and whether exposure-dependent regulatory annotations are enriched for childhood metabolic trait heritability. 2.4 Interpret the findings We plan to report placental xQTL associations across cohorts and ancestry groups, likely causal variants, comparisons across types of RNA measurements, genes and isoforms prioritized at GWAS loci, and genetic effects that vary with gestational exposures. Public results will report combined findings. Cohort-specific results will be shared only as agreed with each participating cohort. 3. Data and computing needed at each cohort The pipeline is intended for cohorts with fetal genotype data (SNP arrays, whole-exome sequencing, or whole-genome sequencing where suitable for downstream imputation and QC) and placental bulk RNA-seq. Broad transcript coverage, such as total RNA-seq, is important for isoform, splicing, transcript-end, and RNA-editing analyses; 3′-capture assays may not support the complete modality set. Data availability and sequencing design will be reviewed with each site before analysis. Each site runs the analyses on its own research computing system using a supplied, self-contained software container that includes the reference data and runs without internet access, which keeps software and reference versions consistent across sites. After approval, MDACC also supplies by email a small restricted file containing the shared splicing reference clusters and the list of MDACC xQTL signals that every site tests for cell-type and exposure interactions. It uses the site’s fetal genotypes, RNA sequencing data, and a limited sample metadata table. Required local metadata are an RNA-seq identifier, genotype identifier, fetal sex, and gestational age at delivery. Optional local metadata include pre-pregnancy BMI, GDM, OGTT glucose, maternal age, parity, and smoking; interaction modules are enabled only when relevant variables and sufficient samples are available. Genotype imputation is required and must be performed through the TOPMed Imputation Server. Each participating site is responsible for uploading quality-controlled genotype files directly to the TOPMed Imputation Server in accordance with its terms of use and the site’s data-governance requirements. \[15\] 6. Files requested from each cohort Each site prepares summary files separately for each eligible ancestry group. Variants are identified by GRCh38 chromosome, position, and reference and alternate alleles. RNA features use the common annotation IDs and coordinates. The files contain no sample identifiers or participant-level records. The main requested results are variant-by-feature effect estimates (betas), standard errors (SEs), p-values, minor-allele frequencies (MAFs), minor-allele counts (MACs), sample sizes, and LD matrices. Data sharing and safeguards Files sent to MDACC exclude individual genotypes or sequencing reads (FASTQ/BAM), participant identifiers, per-sample molecular or clinical data, exposure values, latent factors, or cell-type proportions. Summary results are prepared separately for ancestry groups with at least 50 analyzed samples. MDACC will store approved shared files on access-controlled research computing infrastructure and use them for the collaborative placental xQTL analyses described here. Per-cohort files will not be redistributed or publicly released without the contributing cohort’s agreement. Publicly released findings will combine results across cohorts. Authorship, acknowledgement, access, and any additional uses should be established with collaborators in advance. 8. Setup This page takes a site from nothing to a working installation: get the image, check it, export the launcher, and confirm that the cluster can run the pipeline. It takes about 30 minutes plus the image download. Restricted file: request it before you start. Site runs need xqtl-restricted-<version>.tar.gz, a small file holding the shared (frozen) splicing clusters and the MDACC signal list. It is not in the image or on any public server. MDACC sends it by email to sites with an approved data-sharing agreement. If you have not received it, request it from Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org), stating: your cohort name, the pipeline version you will run (for example 1.0.0), and the approved agreement (title or reference number). Keep the file inside your secure environment and set its path as restricted: in cohort.yml. The smoke test (step 5) reports whether it is present and intact. What you need Requirement Details Linux, x86-64 Login/head node plus compute nodes (or a single large workstation) Apptainer ≥ 1.0 or Singularity ≥ 3.8 On every node that runs tasks. Check with apptainer --version or singularity --version A batch scheduler (optional) LSF, SLURM, PBS Pro/Torque or SGE. See HPC configuration Shared filesystem Visible from the head node and all compute nodes, for the work directory and results Disk The image file (its size is listed on the release page and the Zenodo record), plus work space for your cohort (see HPC configuration) Internet Only to download the image once. Nothing at run time Nothing else is installed on the host: no conda, Java, Nextflow, R or Python. All of them come from the image. 1. Get the image The image is one file, xqtl-federated_<version>.sif, available from two places that hold the same bytes. From the GitHub container registry (needs outbound HTTPS to ghcr.io from the machine you download on): apptainer pull xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif oras://ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:1.0.0 # Singularity: singularity pull xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif oras://ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:1.0.0 From Zenodo (a plain HTTPS download; works through most proxies and can be done on a laptop and copied over): download xqtl-federated_<version>.sif and xqtl-federated_<version>.sif.sha256 from the Zenodo record linked on the GitHub release page. Verify the download. The checksum file is attached to the GitHub release and to the Zenodo record: sha256sum -c xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif.sha256 # must print: xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif: OK Put the .sif on the shared filesystem, for example next to where you will keep the launcher. One copy serves every run; compute nodes read it directly, so no image cache is needed. A Docker image of the same build (ghcr.io/sbresnahan/placenta-xqtl-federated:<version>) exists for workstations and continuous integration. Most clusters do not allow Docker; use the .sif. 2. Check the image apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif help # commands available in the image apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif versions # software versions (TSV) apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif refs-check # verify the embedded reference data (sha256; ~1 min) refs-check compares every embedded reference file with the checksums recorded for this release and ends with OK <n> reference files verified. A failure means the image file is damaged; download it again. 3. Export the launcher (bootstrap) Nextflow’s head job runs on the host, outside the container, so it can submit jobs to your scheduler. bootstrap copies what the head job needs out of the image into a directory you choose: apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif bootstrap ./xqtl Written Contents xqtl/run_xqtl.sh The launcher you run from now on xqtl/pipeline/ Pipeline code (identical to the copy in the image) xqtl/jre/ Java 17 runtime for the head job xqtl/nextflow/ Nextflow launcher (self-contained build) and its home directory xqtl/docs/ This documentation for offline reading: open xqtl/docs/index.html xqtl/VERSIONS.tsv, xqtl/XQTL_VERSION, xqtl/refs_MANIFEST.tsv Software versions, pipeline version, reference checksums The reference data stay inside the image; tasks read them at /opt/xqtl/refs. Notes: The destination must be on a filesystem visible inside the container. Apptainer binds $HOME and the current directory by default; for other locations add -B /path (for example apptainer run -B /scratch xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif bootstrap /scratch/xqtl). bootstrap records the path of the .sif in run_xqtl.sh. If you move the image later, set XQTL_SIF=/new/path/xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif before running, or bootstrap again. Use one directory per pipeline version. bootstrap refuses to write into a directory that already holds an installation; --force replaces the exported files and leaves your own files, work directories and results untouched. If bootstrap says it cannot tell where the .sif is (this happens with some older Singularity versions), add --sif /full/path/xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif. 4. What run_xqtl.sh does run_xqtl.sh runs nextflow run xqtl/pipeline/main.nf --sif <image> <your arguments> with: Setting Value Why JAVA_HOME xqtl/jre No Java needed on the host NXF_HOME xqtl/nextflow/home Nextflow keeps its files inside the installation, not in $HOME/.nextflow NXF_OFFLINE true Nextflow never tries to reach the internet (on seadragon each attempt cost about 130 s) NXF_OPTS -Xms1g -Xmx4g unless you set it Head-job memory; see HPC configuration XQTL_SIF the .sif path Every task runs in this image Any NXF_VER, NXF_JAVA_HOME or JAVA_CMD in your environment is ignored, so a Nextflow or Java installation already on the host cannot interfere. Run it from the directory where you want the work directory and results, usually on scratch: cd /scratch/$USER/xqtl_run /path/to/xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode <mode> Long runs should be launched as a batch job or inside tmux/screen; see Running the head inside a batch job and the templates in pipeline/assets/head_job/. 5. Check that your cluster works (smoke test) /path/to/xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon,smoke --restricted /secure/path/xqtl-restricted-1.tar.gz # other sites: -profile slurm,apptainer,smoke -c conf/sites/<yoursite>.config ... The smoke test takes about 10 minutes and runs 12 checks (container start-up, tools, references, restricted file, job fan-out and arrays, memory enforcement, filesystem binds, a small tensorQTL run). It writes xqtl_smoke/smoke/smoke_summary.tsv ending in VERDICT GO or VERDICT NO-GO. HPC configuration explains each check and what to do about a FAIL or WARN. Send MDACC the summary file if you would like a second opinion; it holds no data. 6. Build the alignment indices (once per site) STAR, Salmon and IRFinder-S indices are too large to ship in the image, so each site builds them once from the references inside it: /path/to/xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode prepare_references The indices are written to site_refs: in cohort.yml and reused by every later run. Expect 1–2 hours and about 32–40 GB of memory; details are in Phenotyping. Upgrading to a new pipeline version Download and verify the new .sif (step 1). Bootstrap it into a new directory, for example ./xqtl-1.1.0. Check the changelog: a new major version changes the export format or the restricted-file version, and MDACC will send a new restricted file. Re-run the smoke test. Site indices from prepare_references are reused unless the changelog says otherwise. Keep the old directory until the new version has run; results record the version that produced them. Offline documentation Every image carries this documentation. After bootstrap, open xqtl/docs/index.html in a browser (copy the folder to a laptop if the cluster has no browser). apptainer run <sif> docs prints its location inside the image. The online copy is at https://sbresnahan.github.io/placenta-xqtl-federated/.

HPC configuration guide This guide explains how the pipeline requests compute resources and how to adapt it to your cluster. Most sites only need to choose a profile, copy one site template and set five or six values. Validate every new configuration with the smoke test (see Validating a new site) before running real data. The pipeline runs in two parts: The head is a small Java process (Nextflow) that runs on a login node, a workflow node or inside a batch job. It submits every task to the scheduler and tracks it. It needs about 1 CPU and 2–4 GB of memory for the whole run, which can take several days. Tasks are batch jobs. Each task runs inside the same pipeline image (a .sif file, run with Apptainer or Singularity) on a compute node. Neither part needs internet access. The image contains all software and public reference data, and run_xqtl.sh (written by the image’s bootstrap command; see Setup) starts Nextflow in offline mode. Configuration layers Resource settings are layered so that the pipeline code never contains anything site-specific: Layer File What it sets Who edits it 1. Process labels modules/, workflows/ Each process declares a resource class (label 'process_medium'), never a queue, account or path Pipeline developers 2. Resource classes conf/base.config CPUs, memory and walltime for each class; retry policy; queue selection rule; caps Rarely changed 3. Executor profile conf/executors/<scheduler>.config Scheduler type, job submission rate, polling Rarely changed 4. Container profile conf/containers/<engine>.config Apptainer, Singularity or Docker; bind paths Rarely changed 5. Site profile conf/sites/<site>.config Queues, account codes, GPU syntax, bind paths, node limits Each site 6. Command line --max_memory 64.GB etc. Overrides any parameter for one run Each run Later layers override earlier ones. Profiles are combined with commas, for example -profile slurm,apptainer, and a site file is added with -c conf/sites/<site>.config. Seadragon has a built-in profile that bundles layers 3–5: -profile seadragon. To see the configuration that a combination resolves to, without running anything: nextflow config -profile slurm,apptainer -c conf/sites/mysite.config . Resource classes Defined in conf/base.config. Memory and time are multiplied by the attempt number, so a task that is killed for exceeding its memory or walltime is resubmitted with twice (then three times) as much. Process names are listed in the execution report (<outdir>/pipeline_info/report_*.html). Caps (--max_cpus, --max_memory, --max_time) Every request is capped at --max_cpus, --max_memory and --max_time (Nextflow process.resourceLimits). Set these to the largest node and longest queue you may use; a request above the cap is lowered to the cap instead of being rejected by the scheduler. Defaults are 16 CPUs, 128 GB and 120 h. Check node sizes with bhosts -l / lshosts (LSF), sinfo -o "%n %c %m" (SLURM), pbsnodes -a (PBS) or qhost (SGE). Executors Scheduler Profile Notes IBM Spectrum LSF lsf Memory is per job (perJobMemLimit); see Memory SLURM slurm --mem per job by default; --mem-per-cpu option in the template PBS Pro / OpenPBS pbspro select=1:ncpus=N:mem=M syntax Torque / PBS pbs nodes=1:ppn=N,mem=M syntax SGE / UGE / Son of Grid Engine sge Uses parallel environment smp; change it if your site uses another name No scheduler (one large node) local All tasks run on the head’s node; capped by --max_cpus / --max_memory Site templates with every value marked EDIT are in conf/sites/: TEMPLATE_slurm.config TEMPLATE_lsf.config TEMPLATE_pbspro.config (also works for Torque with -profile pbs) TEMPLATE_sge.config Copy one to conf/sites/<yoursite>.config, edit it and run with: ./run_xqtl.sh -profile slurm,apptainer -c conf/sites/<yoursite>.config -params-file cohort.yml --mode smoke Single node (-profile local) On a workstation or one large allocated node, -profile local,apptainer runs every task on that machine, never using more than --max_cpus and --max_memory at once. A full cohort needs many CPU-days (see Tuning); this mode suits small cohorts, the smoke test and re-running the export. Queues and partitions Many schedulers reject or misroute jobs whose walltime does not fit the queue. The pipeline chooses a queue for each task from its walltime with --queue_rules: --queue_rules 'short:3h,medium:23h59m,long:120h' Rules are read left to right; the first queue whose limit is at least the task’s walltime is used, and the last queue takes anything longer. Because walltime grows with each retry, a retried task can move to a longer queue automatically. List queues in increasing walltime order. --queue NAME sends every task to one queue and ignores the rules. With neither set, no queue is requested and the scheduler’s default is used. --gpu_queue is used only for GPU tasks with --use_gpu. Find your limits with bqueues -l (LSF), scontrol show partition (SLURM), qstat -Qf (PBS) or qconf -sq <queue> (SGE). Memory The scheduler must receive the same memory number that the task will use, and in the units it expects. Getting this wrong is the most common cause of jobs being killed or never starting. LSF perJobMemLimit = true (the default here, --lsf_per_job_mem true) tells Nextflow that memory limits apply to the whole job. Without it, Nextflow divides the request by the number of CPUs, and multi-core tasks are killed far below their request on clusters configured per job. Nextflow reads LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS from $LSF_ENVDIR/lsf.conf to choose the unit for -M and rusage[mem=...]. The head must therefore run in a shell where the LSF environment is loaded (LSF_ENVDIR set). Check one submitted script (.command.run in any task directory) and confirm that the #BSUB -M value is in the unit your site expects. If LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE=y (as on seadragon), a task that exceeds its request is killed with exit status 130 and retried with more memory. To check how your site is configured: grep -E 'LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS|LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE|LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE|LSB_JOB_MEMLIMIT' $LSF_ENVDIR/lsf.conf SLURM By default the pipeline requests memory per job (--mem). This is correct on almost all SLURM sites. Some sites require --mem-per-cpu. The SLURM template contains a commented clusterOptions line that converts the request; enable it if jobs are rejected with a memory-specification error. Sites that set DefMemPerCPU without enforcing --mem can still kill jobs through cgroups; the smoke test (S10) shows whether memory is enforced. PBS and SGE PBS Pro: memory goes into the select statement (mem=), per job. Torque: -l mem= per job; some Torque sites need pmem (per process) instead. Add it with --cluster_options. SGE: memory is requested with -l h_vmem (per slot on many sites). If your site expects per-slot values, divide the request in your site file: process.clusterOptions = { "-l h_vmem=${(task.memory.toMega() / task.cpus) as int}M" } Retries after memory or time kills conf/base.config retries a task up to 3 times when it exits with a status that schedulers use for resource kills: 104, 130, 134, 137, 139, 140, 143, 247 or 271. Other failures stop the run after running tasks finish (errorStrategy 'finish'), so you can fix the problem and continue with -resume. If a task fails with a resource error on all attempts, raise its class or the cap in your site file rather than editing the pipeline. CPUs and threads Each tool receives the number of CPUs from task.cpus explicitly (for example STAR --runThreadN ${task.cpus}, salmon -p, plink2 --threads, torch.set_num_threads). Tools therefore never use more cores than requested, even on schedulers that do not confine CPUs. The container receives the scheduler’s job variables (LSB_*, SLURM_*, PBS_*, JOB_ID, SGE_TASK_ID, NSLOTS) through the engine’s environment whitelist. Every multi-threaded process also sets OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS to task.cpus, which keeps R and numpy linear algebra within the request. On LSF sites with LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE="cpu" (seadragon), a task only sees the cores it requested; the smoke test reports this (S06 shows nproc equal to the request). Job arrays, queue size and submission rate Job arrays. Processes with many short identical tasks (per-chromosome or per-chunk steps, label process_array) are submitted as job arrays of up to --job_array_size tasks (default 50). This reduces scheduler load and queue wait. Arrays work with LSF, SLURM, PBS Pro and SGE; the local executor ignores them. --job_array_size 0 turns arrays off. --queue_size (default 100; seadragon 200) is the maximum number of jobs Nextflow keeps queued or running at once. Lower it if your site limits jobs per user. --submit_rate_limit (default '10 sec', meaning 10 submissions per second) throttles submission. Use '1 sec' or '30 min'-style values only if the scheduler administrators ask. Polling: status is checked every 30 s and the queue every 2 min, which is gentle on the scheduler. GPUs GPUs are optional. All tensorQTL steps run on CPU by default, which takes longer but needs nothing special. To use GPUs: Use the CUDA image (xqtl-federated_<version>-cuda.sif) through --sif. Add --use_gpu true. Set the GPU queue and request syntax in your site file: Scheduler gpu_cluster_options example LSF -gpu num=1 (seadragon) or -gpu "num=1:mode=shared" SLURM --gres=gpu:1 or --gpus=1 PBS Pro -l select=1:ngpus=1 SGE -l gpu=1 With --use_gpu, tasks labelled process_gpu_capable go to --gpu_queue, request 4 CPUs plus the GPU flags, and Apptainer/Singularity are started with --nv so the container can see the NVIDIA driver. Without it, the same tasks run on CPU with 8 CPUs. Results are numerically equivalent within floating-point tolerance. The smoke test checks GPU tensorQTL only when --use_gpu true is given. Container runtime Apptainer or Singularity Apptainer ≥ 1.0 is recommended (-profile <scheduler>,apptainer). On sites where Apptainer is installed under the name singularity, or where only SingularityCE ≥ 3.8 is available, use -profile <scheduler>,singularity. Seadragon is in this group (Apptainer 1.5 invoked as singularity). Docker (-profile <scheduler>,docker) suits workstations; most clusters do not allow it. The image is a local file. run_xqtl.sh passes its path as --sif, so nothing is pulled at run time and no image cache is needed (NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR and NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR are unused). Bind paths Inside the container, only paths that are bound are visible. autoMounts binds the work directory and the paths of input files automatically, but data reached through symlinks or listed inside a samplesheet often live on other filesystems. List every filesystem that holds FASTQs, genotypes, the restricted file, the work directory and outputs: --bind_paths '/scratch,/project,/data' The smoke test checks a path you choose with --bind_test_path /project/somefile.txt (S09). In a site file, bind_paths, max_cpus, max_memory and max_time take effect through the block at the end of the templates in conf/sites/, which sets apptainer.runOptions, singularity.runOptions and process.resourceLimits from them. Keep that block when you write your own site file: the container and executor profiles are read before the site file, so without it the values set there are not applied. Values given on the command line always apply. Work directory, temporary space and cleanup Work directory (-w). Every task runs in its own subdirectory of the work directory. Put it on a large shared filesystem visible to all compute nodes, ideally scratch: -w /scratch/$USER/xqtl_work. A full cohort produces about 2 TB of transient alignment files at peak. Temporary files. Tasks write temporary files inside their work directory, not to /tmp, because /tmp on compute nodes is often small. To use fast node-local disk instead, set process.scratch = '/local/scratch' (or '$TMPDIR') in your site file; Nextflow then runs each task in that directory and copies outputs back. Apptainer build/temp directories are not used at run time, since nothing is built or pulled. Cleanup. Keep the work directory until the run has finished and the export has been reviewed, because -resume needs it. Then delete it, or run nextflow clean -f -before <last run name> from the launch directory. Intermediate BAMs are deleted by the pipeline once their counts are written. Running offline Compute nodes at most sites have no internet access, and the pipeline never needs it: NXF_OFFLINE=true is set by run_xqtl.sh. Without it, Nextflow tries to contact www.nextflow.io at every launch; on seadragon that added about 130 s per launch before timing out. No plugins. The pipeline uses no Nextflow plugins, so nothing is downloaded at launch. Input validation is done by a Python step inside the image (bin/xqtl_validate.py). The launcher is exported from the image. apptainer run <sif> bootstrap ./xqtl copies the pipeline code, a Java runtime and the Nextflow launcher out of the image, and writes run_xqtl.sh with JAVA_HOME, NXF_HOME and the image path set. The host needs only Apptainer or Singularity and a scheduler. References are inside the image. Processes read the public references from /opt/xqtl/refs inside the container. Indices that must be built for your read length are written once by --mode prepare_references to --site_refs. Running the head inside a batch job Running Nextflow on a login node is fine for short runs, but many sites kill long login-node processes. For full runs, submit the head as an ordinary batch job; it then submits tasks as further jobs. This was confirmed on seadragon (head job on the medium queue). Templates are in assets/head_job/ (lsf.sh, slurm.sh, pbs.sh, sge.sh). The essential settings are: Setting Value Why CPUs 1–2 The head does little computation Memory 4–8 GB Java heap plus headroom NXF_OPTS -Xms1g -Xmx4g Keeps the JVM within the job’s memory limit Walltime Longest queue (e.g. 120 h) The head must outlive all tasks; resume if it is killed Queue One that allows jobs to submit jobs Some sites forbid submission from compute nodes; ask your administrators Example for LSF: #BSUB -J xqtl_head #BSUB -q long #BSUB -W 120:00 #BSUB -n 1 #BSUB -M 8 #BSUB -R "rusage[mem=8]" #BSUB -o xqtl_head.%J.out export NXF_OPTS="-Xms1g -Xmx4g" cd "$LS_SUBCWD" ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon -params-file cohort.yml --mode site -resume If the head job is killed, resubmit it with -resume: finished tasks are reused, and jobs that were still running are resubmitted. Site-specific settings Account, project and QOS codes Put flags required on every job in --cluster_options, usually in your site file: Scheduler Example LSF -P myproject or -G mygroup SLURM --account=myproj --qos=normal PBS -A myproject SGE -P myproject GPU tasks receive both cluster_options and gpu_cluster_options. Module systems Nothing needs to be loaded inside tasks, because all software is in the image. On the head node, Apptainer or Singularity must be on PATH for the head and for the batch jobs. If your site provides it as a module, add module load apptainer to your shell profile or to the head job script, and add process.beforeScript = 'module load apptainer' to your site file if compute nodes do not inherit it. Validating a new site Before running real data, run the smoke test with exactly the profile you will use for real runs: ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon,smoke --bind_test_path /rsrch5/home/$USER/somefile.txt \ --restricted /path/to/xqtl-restricted-1.tar.gz For other sites: -profile slurm,apptainer,smoke -c conf/sites/mysite.config. Then run the same command again with -resume; every task should be reported as cached. The test takes 5–15 minutes, depending on queue wait, and uses only synthetic data generated inside the tasks. Results are written to xqtl_smoke/smoke/smoke_summary.tsv, ending with VERDICT GO or NO-GO: Test What it checks If it fails S01 container R The image starts on compute nodes; R 4.3.1 runs Engine not on PATH on compute nodes; wrong --sif path; image not readable from nodes S02 embedded tools Every tool in the image reports a version (tool_versions.tsv) Wrong or damaged image; re-verify the sha256 S03 embedded references Reference files match the image manifest Wrong image or --refs_dir S04 restricted file The restricted file opens, has the expected version and checksums WARN if not given; FAIL if damaged or the wrong version. Request it by email (see Setup) S05 plink2 Genotype tooling runs Image problem S06 resources 4 CPUs and 8 GB are granted; a 4 GB allocation succeeds; whether CPUs are confined (scheduler view in sched_view.txt) Memory units or per-job/per-slot setting wrong (see Memory) S07 fan-out 5 independent jobs run, usually on several nodes Queue or account settings S08 job array A 5-task job array runs Arrays disabled at your site: set --job_array_size 0 S09 bind read A file on your project filesystem is visible in the container Add the filesystem to --bind_paths S10 memory enforcement and retry A task that exceeds its 2 GB request is killed and retried with 4 GB WARN means memory is not enforced; set --max_memory conservatively S11 tensorQTL CPU (or GPU with --use_gpu) cis-mapping recovers a planted signal Image or GPU driver problem S12 Storey q-value The R qvalue bridge runs on tensorQTL output Image problem WARN and SKIP lines do not block a GO, but they tell you which defaults to adjust. Send the summary file to MDACC with your first export. Worked example: seadragon (MD Anderson) Seadragon runs IBM LSF with Apptainer 1.5.1, invoked as singularity. The built-in profile conf/sites/seadragon.config encodes the results of the cluster checks run there (Testing and validation): includeConfig '../executors/lsf.config' includeConfig '../containers/singularity.config' params { queue_rules = 'short:3h,medium:23h59m,long:120h' gpu_queue = 'gpu' gpu_cluster_options = '-gpu num=1' bind_paths = '/rsrch5,/rsrch9' max_cpus = 16 max_memory = '120.GB' max_time = '120.h' queue_size = 200 } executor { perJobMemLimit = true } // set again from the params above (see Bind paths) process.resourceLimits = [cpus: params.max_cpus as int, memory: params.max_memory as nextflow.util.MemoryUnit, time: params.max_time as nextflow.util.Duration] singularity.runOptions = '-B /rsrch5 -B /rsrch9' // derived from bind_paths Why each value: Queues. Seadragon’s submission filter (esub) rejects walltimes outside each queue’s range: short ≤ 3 h, medium more than 3 h and under 24 h, long 24–120 h. The rule medium:23h59m keeps 24-hour tasks out of medium. Memory. LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS=GB and LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE=y: memory is per job, in GB, and enforced. In the cluster checks, the over-limit task was killed with exit 130 and retried successfully with 4 GB. CPUs. LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE="cpu gpu" confines each job to its requested cores (nproc=4 for a 4-core request). Bind paths. Project data live on /rsrch5 and /rsrch9. Network. Compute nodes have no internet. Of the container registries, ghcr.io and quay.io were reachable from login nodes at about 0.6 MB/s; Docker Hub, gcr.io and Amazon ECR were blocked or unreliable. Download the SIF once (about 3–4 h at that speed) or copy it by Globus. Building images. apptainer build --fakeroot with package installation fails on seadragon (apt exit 100). Never build images there; use the published SIF. Head. Both a login-node head and a head inside an LSF job (medium queue, 1 core, 4 GB) passed the cluster checks. Tuning table Approximate requirements for one cohort of about 350 samples with about 50 M read pairs each: Stage Class Jobs Typical CPU-hours Peak disk Index build (prepare_references, once) process_high + process_high_memory 3 30–60 60 GB STAR + Salmon per sample process_medium ~700 1,000–1,800 ~2 TB BAMs (transient) Junctions, featureCounts, editing pileups, IRFinder-S process_low/process_medium ~1,400 400–700 200 GB Aggregation, normalization, MuSiC process_medium/process_high ~40 50–100 50 GB HCP grid (per modality × ancestry) process_medium ~60 ~60 small tensorQTL (per modality × ancestry) process_gpu_capable ~50 100–300 (CPU) 100 GB GxE scans, tiers 1 and 2 (per ancestry × modality × exposure × tier × chromosome) process_gpu_capable ~800 per exposure 100–300 (CPU) tier 2: see below G×C, GxE merge and sensitivity, LD, export process_medium/process_low ~150 20–50 100–150 GB export GxE tier 2 stores every cis variant of the test-set phenotypes, so for those phenotypes its size grows like file A. If a site cannot hold or share it, gxe.tier2: pairs keeps only the lead variants (Interaction analyses). To shorten runs, raise --queue_size (if allowed), use GPUs for tensorQTL, and place the work directory on the fastest shared filesystem. Configuration Cohort settings are written in one YAML file, cohort.yml, and passed with -params-file. Cluster settings (queues, memory, bind paths) belong in a site profile, not here; see HPC configuration. ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode <mode> Any setting can also be given on the command line (--outdir /scratch/run2), which overrides the file. Nested settings are easier to keep in the file. Every mode starts by checking cohort.yml and the input files against the schema (assets/schema/cohort.schema.json). The run stops before any task is submitted if a check fails. The report is written to <outdir>/pipeline_info/validation_report.tsv, and the complete settings with every default filled in are written to resolved_params.json in the same folder. To run only the checks: ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode site --validate_only Troubleshooting explains each message. A minimal cohort.yml cohort_id: COHORT1 # letters, digits, _ or -; used in file names outdir: /scratch/xqtl/COHORT1 # visible to compute nodes samplesheet: samplesheet.csv metadata: metadata.tsv restricted: /secure/xqtl-restricted-1.tar.gz site_refs: /project/xqtl/site_refs # written once by --mode prepare_references genotypes: raw: /project/geno/array_merged # PLINK prefix, VCF or BCF (only for --mode imputation_prep) raw_build: GRCh37 source: array imputed_dir: /project/geno/topmed_r3 # decrypted TOPMed output (for --mode site) rnaseq: read_layout: paired strandedness: reverse read_length: 150 library_type: total Everything else has a default. Relative paths in cohort.yml are resolved from the launch directory; relative FASTQ paths in the samplesheet are resolved from the samplesheet’s folder. Walkthrough 1. Setup and smoke test 2. Input tables and cohort.yml 3. Genotypes for imputation 4. TOPMed imputation 5. Site indices (once per site) 6. Site analysis 7. Review the export 8. Transfer 9. Central analysis (MDACC)

Walkthrough This page follows one cohort from raw data to the files it shares, and then the MDACC side. Each step links to the page with the details. Step Who Mode Result 1. Setup and smoke test site smoke VERDICT GO 2. Input tables and cohort.yml site --validate_only a clean validation report 3. Genotypes for imputation site imputation_prep per-chromosome GRCh38 VCFs and a TOPMed checklist 4. TOPMed imputation site manual upload decrypted chr*.dose.vcf.gz 5. Site indices (once) site prepare_references site_refs/ 6. Site analysis site site <outdir>/export/<cohort_id>/ 7. Review the export site — approval to share 8. Transfer site → MDACC Globus or agreed method received export 9. Central analysis MDACC central meta-analysis, fine-mapping, colocalization, TWAS inputs 1. Setup and smoke test Follow Setup: download and verify the image, run bootstrap, choose or write a site profile (HPC configuration), then run the smoke test until it reports VERDICT GO. Keep the restricted file sent by MDACC in a location only your team can read. All later commands are run from a working folder on scratch, with the head process inside a batch job or tmux (Running the head inside a batch job): cd /scratch/$USER/xqtl_COHORT1 XQTL=/project/xqtl/xqtl-1.0.0 # the bootstrap folder 2. Input tables and cohort.yml Prepare the samplesheet, the metadata table and cohort.yml as described in Configuration. Then check them: $XQTL/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode site --validate_only Read <outdir>/pipeline_info/validation_report.tsv. Every FAIL must be fixed; read each WARN (Troubleshooting). Before imputation, genotypes.imputed_dir does not exist yet, so required.genotypes.imputed_dir fails; every other check should pass. The same command with --mode imputation_prep checks the raw genotypes. 3. Genotypes for imputation $XQTL/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode imputation_prep This reads genotypes.raw (VCF/BCF or PLINK, GRCh37 or GRCh38, array, WES or WGS) and writes to <outdir>/imputation_prep/: chr1.vcf.gz … chr22.vcf.gz: biallelic SNPs on GRCh38, REF/ALT aligned to the reference, filtered with the imputation_prep settings; imputation_prep_report.tsv: variant counts after each filter and the reference-match rate; imputation_prep_samples.tsv: per-sample missingness and the chrX sex check against the metadata; liftover_summary.tsv (GRCh37 input only); TOPMED_CHECKLIST.md: the upload settings for this cohort. Check the reports before uploading. A reference-match rate below imputation_prep.ref_match_min stops the run with “Wrong build?” and publishes no VCF; see Troubleshooting. Samples whose genotype sex disagrees with the metadata may be swapped; resolve them before imputation. 4. TOPMed imputation The upload is manual and follows your institution’s approval for sending genotypes to the TOPMed Imputation Server. Follow TOPMED_CHECKLIST.md: reference panel TOPMed R3 on GRCh38; array build GRCh38; rsq filter off; phasing with Eagle v2.4; mode Quality Control & Imputation; the one-time password for the results arrives by email and cannot be re-sent; results are deleted from the server after 7 days. Unzip the results into one folder and set genotypes.imputed_dir (and imputed_pattern if your file names differ from chr{chr}.dose.vcf.gz). 5. Site indices (once per site) $XQTL/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode prepare_references This builds the STAR, Salmon and IRFinder-S indices into site_refs (Phenotyping). It is reused by later runs and pipeline versions unless the changelog says otherwise. Skip this step if you supply ready phenotypes with phenotypes_dir. 6. Site analysis $XQTL/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode site The run goes through: phenotyping from FASTQs: nine modalities and cell-type proportions (Phenotyping); post-imputation genotype QC and ancestry assignment; per ancestry group with at least ancestry.min_n samples: normalization, hidden factors, cis-xQTL mapping, conditional analysis and LD; G×C and GxE interaction tests (Interaction analyses); the export with its leak scan (Export specification). If the run stops (a failed task, a killed head process, a maintenance window), fix the cause and run the same command with -resume from the same folder; finished tasks are not repeated. Outputs: Folder Content Shared? <outdir>/phenotypes/ Phenotype BEDs, QC metrics, cell-type proportions No <outdir>/site/ Genotype QC, ancestry, per-stratum mapping, interaction results and diagnostics No <outdir>/pipeline_info/ Validation report, settings, Nextflow trace and reports, leak_report.tsv No <outdir>/export/<cohort_id>/ Files A–J Yes, after review 7. Review the export Before anything is shared, the site team reviews export/<cohort_id>/: <cohort_id>_cohort_I_strata.tsv: which ancestry groups were mapped and exported, and which were below ancestry.min_n; DATA_DICTIONARY.md: every column of every file; MANIFEST.tsv: every file with its size, row count and sha256, the pipeline and restricted-file versions and the image checksum; the leak scan passed: otherwise there is no export folder, and pipeline_info/leak_report.tsv has only its header line. The Export specification lists what is never exported. If the cohort wants different rounding or a minimum minor-allele count in file A, change export.round_digits or export.min_mac_export and rebuild the export without recomputing anything: $XQTL/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode export 8. Transfer Send only the export/<cohort_id>/ folder, by the method agreed with MDACC (for example Globus), keeping its structure. Expect roughly 100–150 GB per ancestry group, mostly files A and C. Tell MDACC the release tag and the sha256 of MANIFEST.tsv: sha256sum export/COHORT1/MANIFEST.tsv 9. Central analysis (MDACC) MDACC stores each received export in its own dated folder, verifies MANIFEST.tsv, adds the study to studies.tsv and runs --mode central (Central analysis). Ingest checks every checksum again and stops if a file is missing or changed, or if the exports were made with incompatible pipeline versions. MDACC shares combined results with the cohorts; per-cohort files are not redistributed (Collaboration brief).

Phenotyping This page describes how a site’s RNA-seq FASTQs become the nine molecular phenotypes that are mapped by --mode site. The steps build on Pantry (MIT licence, LICENSES/PANTRY-MIT.txt). Implementation choices are listed at the end. Phenotyping runs in two modes: --mode site, when phenotypes_dir is not set: FASTQs → phenotypes → genotype QC, mapping and export. --mode phenotyping_only: FASTQs → phenotype BEDs and normalized matrices, without genotypes. Nothing is exported. Use it to check RNA-seq processing before genotypes are ready, or to look at the cohort’s phenotypes locally. Before the first run: site indices run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode prepare_references This builds the aligner and quantifier indices once, from the public references embedded in the image, and writes them to site_refs:. Expect 1–2 hours; STAR’s genome generation needs about 32–40 GB of memory. Directory in site_refs Content genome/ GRCh38 analysis set FASTA, .fai, Picard .dict annotation/ HPLRv2 annotation (header lines removed), exonic / intronic GTFs for stability, Picard refFlat.txt, gene GC content and length star/ STAR index with the annotation’s junctions, --sjdbOverhang = rnaseq.read_length − 1 salmon/expression/ Salmon index of the annotation’s transcripts (gffread) salmon/txrevise.grp_{1,2}.{upstream,downstream}/ Salmon indices of the txrevise alternative transcript-start and transcript-end events irfinder/IRFinder/ IRFinder-S reference (from the STAR index, with mapability exclusion) editing/ REDIportal sites on the annotation’s chromosomes and their genes (only if the REDIportal table is present) MANIFEST.tsv pipeline version, read length, sha256 of every input, tool versions Rebuild the indices if rnaseq.read_length changes a lot; the validator warns when the two differ. Alignment still works with a different read length. Inputs samplesheet: CSV with sample_id,fastq_1,fastq_2. Leave fastq_2 empty for single-end data. Relative paths are resolved from the samplesheet’s directory. sample_id must match rnaseq_id in the metadata. rnaseq in cohort.yml: read_layout (paired / single), strandedness (reverse / forward / unstranded), read_length and library_type (total / polyA / 3prime). restricted: the restricted file from MDACC. Phenotyping uses its frozen splicing clusters. FASTQs are used as delivered: there is no adapter or quality trimming. STAR soft-clips adapter read-through. Per-sample steps Step Tool and settings Alignment STAR 2-pass (--twopassMode Basic --outSAMstrandField intronMotif), coordinate-sorted BAM Gene / transcript quantification Salmon quant -l A --validateMappings --numBootstraps 20 txrevise events Salmon against each of the 4 txrevise indices Junctions regtools junctions extract -a 8 -m 50 -M 500000 -s XS Exonic / intronic reads featureCounts on exonic (-t exon --fracOverlap 1) and intronic (-t intron) GTFs, strand from rnaseq.strandedness, -p for paired-end Intron retention IRFinder-S BAM mode RNA editing per-site editing levels at REDIportal sites (MAPQ 255, base quality ≥ 20) Sequencing QC Picard CollectAlignmentSummaryMetrics, MarkDuplicates metrics, CollectGcBiasMetrics, CollectInsertSizeMetrics (paired-end) and CollectRnaSeqMetrics Cohort-level phenotypes Modality How it is built expression Salmon transcript counts (bootstrap-based quantification-uncertainty correction) summarised to genes with tximport. Gene TPM goes into expression.bed.gz; raw counts into expression.counts.bed.gz, which normalization uses for TMM-VST isoform_expression transcript TPM, grouped by gene. Raw transcript counts are in isoform_expression.counts.bed.gz isoform_usage transcript TPM / gene TPM, grouped by gene alt_tss txrevise upstream event usage (groups 1 and 2) alt_polya txrevise downstream event usage (groups 1 and 2) splicing leafCutter intron excision ratios in frozen and novel clusters (below) intron_retention IRFinder-S IR ratios of clean introns, grouped by gene rna_editing editing levels at sites covered ≥ 20 reads in at least max(10, 10 % of samples), collapsing sites that correlate above 0.9 stability exonic / intronic read ratio per gene All BEDs use the gene TSS as coordinates (start = TSS − 1, end = TSS), and features of grouped modalities are named GENE__feature. qc_metrics.tsv has the Picard metrics plus SubjectBias.GC and SubjectBias.GENE_LENGTH (per-sample Pearson correlation of log2(TPM + 1) with gene exonic GC content and length; Mostafavi et al. 2013). A metric missing for a sample is replaced by the cohort median. Splicing: frozen and novel clusters Splicing phenotypes are only comparable between studies if every site uses the same leafCutter clusters. The restricted file therefore holds a frozen cluster set (splicing/frozen_clusters.tsv.gz, IDs clu_<n>_<strand>). Each site: counts its junction reads in the frozen clusters (leafCutter with the frozen clusters as the refined cluster file); clusters its junctions locally (--maxintronlen 100000 --minclureads 30 --mincluratio 0.001); keeps local clusters that share no junction with the frozen set, renamed nclu_<n>_<strand>. Phenotype IDs are GENE__chrom_start_end_clu_<n>_<strand>; novel clusters carry nclu_. Novel-cluster junctions are mapped and exported like the others, and the novel column of the splicing features file flags them. Only junctions in frozen clusters can be meta-analysed across studies; novel clusters are cohort-specific. splicing.clusters_summary.tsv counts the frozen, matched and novel clusters. Cell-type proportions MuSiC estimates cell-type proportions for each RNA-seq sample from gene TPM, using the placental single-cell reference embedded in the image. cell_proportions.tsv has 8 collapsed cell groups (used as covariates and for G×C); cell_proportions_full.tsv has every reference cell type, and maternal_flag.tsv marks samples whose maternal-cell fraction is above 10 %. Library types 3prime libraries only produce expression and stability. polyA libraries produce all modalities, but intronic signal (stability, intron retention) is weaker than in total RNA. rna_editing is skipped when site_refs has no REDIportal sites. Outputs Path Content <outdir>/phenotypes/ <modality>.bed.gz (+ .tbi), the two count BEDs, qc_metrics.tsv, cell proportions, splicing.clusters_summary.tsv, PHENOTYPES_SUMMARY.tsv (features and samples per file) <outdir>/normalized/ --mode phenotyping_only only: ALL_<modality>.bed.gz normalized across all samples (columns are genotype IDs), with phenotype_groups.txt for grouped modalities <outdir>/site/ALL/ --mode phenotyping_only only: normalization diagnostics (outliers, feature lists) <outdir>/phenotypes/ has the layout phenotypes_dir expects, so a later --mode site run can map it directly. None of these files leave the site. Implementation notes Area Choice Why Intron retention IRFinder-S MAJIQ’s licence does not allow redistribution in the image Splicing clusters frozen MDACC clusters + site-specific novel clusters sites cannot pool junctions BAMs for regtools / featureCounts full BAMs one BAM per sample, fewer steps Salmon expression index annotation transcripts from gffread, no decoy sequences built from the image’s references at each site Picard separate Java environment in the image dependency conflict IRFinder-S memory check lowered (IRFINDER_MIN_RAM_MB) the stock check refuses to run below 32 GB even when far less is needed txrevise sets upstream / downstream indexed; the contained sets are shipped but not indexed as in Pantry Cell proportions one estimate per RNA-seq sample consistent with the other phenotypes Small feature sets VST dispersion fit on all features when fewer than 1,000 have mean count > 5 only affects single-chromosome runs

interactions.html
Interaction analyses (G×C and GxE) Test sets G×C: cell-type interaction GxE: exposure interaction Analyses not run at the sites Caveats

Interaction analyses (G×C and GxE) --mode site runs two interaction analyses in every mapped ancestry stratum after cis mapping: G×C: genotype × cell-type proportion at lead xQTL pairs. Exported as file G. GxE: genotype × maternal or pregnancy exposure (gestational age by default). Exported as file H. Both reuse the stratum’s normalized phenotypes, genotypes and final mapping covariates; nothing is re-normalized. Settings are in the gxc and gxe blocks of cohort.yml. Both analyses are on by default. Turn one off with enabled: false. The run state of each stratum is in the gxc and gxe columns of <cohort>_cohort_I_strata.tsv: tested; disabled; no_cell_proportions (G×C only); stratum_below_min_n. Test sets The test sets are built per stratum and modality from two sources: the site’s own leads; the MDACC signal list in the restricted file (mdacc_signals.tsv.gz: MDACC lead pairs per discovery ancestry). Site leads. These are the top variants of phenotypes with q ≤ 0.05 in the stratum’s feature-level permutation table: the expression table for expression and the <modality>_ungrouped table for the other modalities. G×C pairs (leads only). The union of: site leads; MDACC pairs with signal_rank = 1 from any discovery ancestry. Every pair is tested in every stratum, whatever ancestry it was discovered in. source is site, mdacc or both; both means the same phenotype and variant. mdacc_ancestry records the discovery ancestry. A pair that cannot be tested is kept with untested_reason: phenotype_absent: the phenotype is not in the stratum after filtering; variant_absent: the variant did not pass the stratum’s genotype QC. GxE tier-2 phenotypes. Site-lead phenotypes plus every phenotype in the MDACC list (any rank). All cis variants of each one are tested. The site-lead and MDACC-lead variants are flagged (site_lead_variant, mdacc_lead_variant). Intron retention. The MDACC list gives intron-retention signals as MAJIQ segments; sites use IRFinder-S introns (Phenotyping). An MDACC segment is matched to the shortest site intron of the same gene, chromosome and strand that contains it. The original ID is kept in mdacc_phenotype_id. G×C: cell-type interaction For each pair and target cell type, an OLS model with a t-test: Y ~ 1 + g0 + c0 + g0:c0 + Z Term Definition Y the stratum’s normalized phenotype g0 ALT dosage, centred over the analysed samples c0 arcsinh(cell proportion), centred over the stratum, then re-centred over the analysed samples. Proportions are averaged over technical replicates Z the modality’s final mapping covariates, without the target’s own cell-type covariate. Covariates that are constant in the analysed samples are dropped Targets. Every cell type in cell_proportions.tsv except gxc.exclude_cell_types (default Maternal, the decidual fraction). Maternal sensitivity. The same fit is repeated after removing samples whose maternal proportion is above gxc.maternal_threshold (default 0.10). These results are in the maternal_sensitivity_* columns. Fit status. One of: ok; no_common_samples; insufficient_n (fewer than gxc.min_n complete samples, default 20); monomorphic; no_celltype_variation; rank_deficient; insufficient_df; invalid_se. Multiple testing. BH q (q_GxC) over the ok tests, within stratum × modality. Annotation. One row per pair. best_cell_type is the cell type with the smallest (q, p). primary_cell_type is the best cell type if its q ≤ gxc.fdr (default 0.05), otherwise unassigned. Annotation is per pair, not per phenotype: a phenotype with a site pair and a different MDACC pair has two rows. Effects are also reported on an interpretable scale: beta_GxC_iqr: the interaction per interquartile range of the transformed proportion; beta_G_at_cell_q25/q50/q75: the genetic effect at the proportion quartiles; cell_prop_raw_q25/q50/q75: the quartiles of the raw proportion. G×C needs cell-type proportions. Without them, G×C is skipped and I_strata records no_cell_proportions. Proportions come from MuSiC when phenotyping runs, or from phenotypes_dir/cell_proportions.tsv. GxE: exposure interaction Exposures Each enabled exposure in gxe.exposures is read from its metadata column and processed in five steps: averaged over technical replicates; filtered to min–max on the raw scale; transformed (none, log or inverse_normal); continuous exposures are z-scored across all samples of the mapped strata; binary exposures (0/1) are left unscaled. Pooling the scale across strata puts every stratum’s b_GxE on one scale for the central meta-analysis. An exposure is used in a stratum only if both conditions hold: n ≥ gxe.min_n (default 50); for binary exposures, at least gxe.min_cases (default 20) cases and controls. Otherwise its status is insufficient_n or insufficient_cases, and every component is SKIPPED. The exposure summary (H_exposures) gives n, the raw-unit mean and SD, the pooled scale, and counts and prevalence for binary exposures. The per-sample table stays at the site. Defaults: GA is enabled; ppBMI, gdm and ogtt are defined but off. You can add other exposures with the same fields. The validator fails if an enabled exposure has no metadata column. Model Y = b_g G + b_e E + b_gi (G × E) + Z γ + ε Term Definition Y the normalized phenotype, z-scored within the stratum G hard calls (default), or dosages with gxe.dosages: true E the exposure Z the final mapping covariates. A covariate named like the exposure is dropped The model is fitted per cis variant (±1 Mb). The algebra is tensorQTL’s calculate_interaction_nominal: covariates are residualized out with a QR projection; dof = n − k − 4. Variant filters: MAF ≥ 0.01 in the analysed samples; MAF ≥ gxe.maf_interaction (default 0.05) in both halves of the sorted exposure, so that the interaction is estimable. The scans are sharded by chromosome. The scans use the process label process_gpu_capable, so with --use_gpu they run on GPU nodes (HPC). Tier 1: permutation scan of every phenotype Every phenotype is tested; its statistic is the top cis variant for the interaction term. Significance comes from adaptive phenotype permutations: blocks are given by gxe.tier1_permutation_blocks, default 100, 400, 500 and 9,000 (cumulative 100, 500, 1,000 and 10,000); a further block runs only while the running empirical p ≤ 0.10; the null distribution is Beta-approximated (pval_beta), as in tensorQTL map_cis. Phenotype i uses the seed gxe.seed + i, so results do not depend on sharding. Storey q-values (qval) are computed within stratum × modality × exposure, with a BH fallback recorded in qvalue_method. A non-finite pval_beta gives q = 1. Tier 2: all cis variants of the test-set phenotypes Nominal interaction statistics are reported for every cis variant of every tier-2 phenotype. The central workflow combines them across strata and cohorts by inverse-variance weighting. af, b_gi, b_gi_se and tstat_gi are stored as float32. gxe.tier2: pairs keeps only the flagged lead variants. It is a fallback for sites that cannot store or share the full table. It is not the default, because the central analysis then cannot test variants the site did not flag. Phenotypes or lead variants that cannot be tested are listed in H_gxe_tier2_untested, with one of these reasons: phenotype_absent; variant_absent; outside_cis_window; the exposure status. top_variant marks the variant with the smallest nominal p for each phenotype. q_top_bh is the BH q over these per-phenotype minima within the stratum. It is not corrected for the number of variants in each window, so it is anti-conservative. Read it as a descriptive summary only; the same applies to the tier-2 n_sig in H_status. Tier-2 inference is made centrally. Sensitivity: SNP × covariate refits Tier-1 hits with q ≤ gxe.fdr are refitted with extra genotype × covariate terms: Y = G + E + G:E + Σ_j G:C_j + covariates Each C_j is an enabled entry of gxe.sensitivity: maternal_age, parity, smoking or GA read a metadata column, which also enters as a main effect; ancestry_pcs uses the genotype PCs already in the covariates, as interactions only. All entries are off by default. The validator fails if an enabled covariate has no numeric metadata column. A hit is stable if the adjusted interaction changes by at most 20 % of the unadjusted one and stays on the same side of p = 0.05. delta_b and rel_change give the change. Run status H_status has one row per stratum × modality × exposure × component (tier1, tier2, sensitivity). Each row has n, the number of covariates, the residual dof, the number tested and the number significant. Status values: Status Meaning DONE the component ran SKIPPED the exposure failed min_n or min_cases in this stratum OFF sensitivity only: no covariate enabled BLOCKED sensitivity only: an enabled covariate’s column is missing Analyses not run at the sites Analysis Reason Transmitted vs non-transmitted allele interactions needs parent–offspring trios, which most cohorts do not have Diagnostics of the G×C model (HC3 robust SEs, permutation calibration, downsampling) run centrally if needed; the site fits use classical OLS standard errors Caveats Power. Interaction tests need far more samples than main-effect tests. In strata near the minimum size, expect only very large interactions to reach significance. Their value is in the central meta-analysis, which is why every stratum reports full tier-2 statistics regardless of significance. Phenotype permutation in tier 1 is slightly conservative for the interaction null when a main genetic effect exists. tensorQTL’s interaction mode uses the same scheme. Exposure scale. The z-scale is pooled within a cohort, not across cohorts. H_exposures reports the pooled mean and SD in raw units, so that b_GxE can be put on a common scale across cohorts centrally. Splicing interactions. Quantile normalization and the inverse normal transform across a cluster’s introns attenuate splicing interaction effects strongly, so splicing interactions need larger strata to be detected than expression interactions.

Per-sample values of any kind: genotypes, dosages, phenotypes, covariates, exposures, cell-type proportions, genotype or HCP PCs, ancestry assignments, outlier lists. Minimum or maximum values. The site keeps these under <outdir>/site/ for its own records. Leak scan The leak scan runs at the end of every export and cannot be disabled. It collects every identifier from: the metadata columns rnaseq_id and genotype_id; the samplesheet sample_id column; all sample IDs in the imputed VCFs. It then checks every exported file. The export fails if any of the following is found: an identifier in a file name, a column name or any text value. Identifiers are matched as whole tokens, so S001 matches reads_S001 but not S0010. Purely numeric or very short IDs are matched only as a complete value. Variant IDs are exempt; an .npz file that holds anything other than one square matrix R; a file type other than Parquet, TSV, gzipped TSV, NPZ, JSON or Markdown. When the scan fails, the export folder is deleted and the run stops. The findings are written to leak_report.tsv in the task work directory; it is local only and must not be shared. Fix the cause, then rebuild the export with --mode export. Rebuilding the export --mode export rebuilds export/ from a finished site run without recomputing anything, for example after changing export.format or export.round_digits.
